note: Language and community education supplement: four distinct substantive works, with selected scopes recorded below. No main data, site, or publication was changed. Source annotations and associated proposed prose have each been kept below 200 derived words per copyrighted work.
minimumCountRecommendation: Four substantive works. The 2009 print and 2018 web lessons are one teaching work, and the dictionary scan and institutional catalogue are one dictionary work. Other leads listed in the evidence file are excluded from the source count.

sources.title: Mentasta Ahtna Language Lessons, second edition (2009; web edition 2018)
sources.publisher: Mt. Sanford Tribal Consortium, Native Language Program; web edition hosted by Frostline Productions
sources.author: Katie John, featured speaker; linguistic transcription by John T. Ritter and James Kari; series editor Cynthea L. Ainsworth
sources.annotation: A substantial teaching work, not a programme directory. Inspected the credits, foreword, preface, introduction, and September–February text units, including conversational drills and grammar charts. The second print edition is dated 2009; the web introduction is April 2018 and web version June 2018. This documents Katie John’s Mentasta variety and named teaching collaborators. Embedded audio was not independently listened to or playback-audited.

sources.title: The Digital Archiving of Endangered Language Oral Traditions: Kaipuleohone at the University of Hawai‘i and C’ek’aedi Hwnax in Alaska
sources.author: Andrea L. Berez
sources.annotation: Read the complete short article, especially printed pp. 261–267 on the Ahtna Heritage Foundation archive, family consultation, access decisions, and the August 2013 learning workshop. The author participated in archive work and credits Foundation collaborators. It describes practice at that time; it does not verify current access arrangements. Public discussion of an archive does not establish permission to redistribute its recordings.

sources.title: Native Perspectives on Sustainability: Kathryn Martin (Ahtna)
sources.author: Kathryn Martin, interviewee; David E. Hall, interviewer; Derek Valldejuli-Gardner, transcriber
sources.annotation: Public interview dated June 22, 2007. Inspected printed pp. 1–4 and 6–7: family mentorship, learning through observation, selective sharing, and educational hopes. This is Martin’s situated first-person account, not a statement binding all Ahtna families. Its project abbreviation “NPS” means Native Perspectives on Sustainability, not the National Park Service. Audio was not audited; ceremonial and taboo details are not reproduced.

sources.title: Ahtna Athabaskan Dictionary
sources.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks; printing partly supported by Ahtna, Inc.; public scan hosted by Alaska Beacon
sources.author: James Kari, compiler and editor, with numerous named Ahtna contributors
sources.annotation: 1990 work, not a 2024 edition. Inspected title and copyright pages; preface vii–viii; acknowledgments ix–x; introduction pp. 9–11; and dialect discussion p. 20. The scan has 710 PDF pages; no claim is made to have read all entries. Kari credits many Ahtna contributors and explicitly describes the dictionary as incomplete. Historical speaker counts are not current estimates.

proposedParagraphs.title: A teaching resource with a named voice and place
proposedParagraphs.text: The Mentasta lessons feature Katie John’s recorded Upper Ahtna speech, with transcription by John T. Ritter and James Kari and editing by Cynthea L. Ainsworth. Their monthly sequence connects conversation with seasonal activities, then develops vocabulary and grammatical patterns through questions and answers. The inspected units cover weather, food, family, everyday activities, and learning to understand the language. The introduction also credits intergenerational teaching work in Mentasta. Readers should approach this as a resource grounded in a particular speaker and variety, rather than assume that every pronunciation or expression represents every Ahtna community. The 2018 web version preserves a teaching work published in 2009.

proposedParagraphs.title: Archives as places for community learning
proposedParagraphs.text: Berez’s 2013 study shows how the Ahtna Heritage Foundation’s C’ek’aedi Hwnax connected preservation with active learning. Its account of an August 2013 workshop brings learners, elders, and linguists together to work with archived recordings, transcription, grammar, and dictionary use. The study also documents local control over access: staff consulted families about legacy recordings whose original permissions could be unclear. These are historical descriptions of the archive’s decisions, rather than confirmation of today’s procedures. The wider lesson is practical: a recording’s survival and a researcher’s ability to describe it do not by themselves settle who may hear it, copy it, or publish it.

proposedParagraphs.title: Learning through relationships and observation
proposedParagraphs.text: In her 2007 interview, Kathryn Martin describes time spent traveling with her grandmother Katie John as a central part of her education. Watching relatives and listening over time connected knowledge with responsibilities to land and people. Martin also discusses the choices facing younger generations and her hopes for schooling that makes room for Ahtna language and culture alongside other educational opportunities. Her account resists reducing education to a textbook or a short list of cultural facts. She explicitly considers the consequences of sharing knowledge outside the community. This is one person’s public reflection at a particular moment, and its examples should retain her attribution and date.

proposedParagraphs.title: A dictionary built through collaboration
proposedParagraphs.text: Kari’s 1990 dictionary makes its Ahtna contributors visible, including Katie and Fred John Sr., Chief Jim McKinley, Mildred Buck, Ruth Johns, and speakers from several regions. Its historical introduction credits Buck, Jeff Leer, Michael Krauss, and Kari with establishing the writing system in 1973, and describes Buck’s work training other Ahtna writers. The dictionary combines roots, affixes, and examples with an English index. Its regional labels help readers recognize variation; they should be read within that work’s framework. Kari also acknowledges missing words and possible errors. The book is therefore a substantial learning and research tool whose own introduction invites correction and continuing community knowledge.

integrationNotes: Use named Mentasta/Upper Ahtna and source-specific regional labels. The lesson series mentions five dialects; Kari 1990 describes four regional dialects. Do not impose either numerical scheme as a timeless universal classification or identify all Chistochina speech automatically as Mentasta.
Do not treat historical estimates in Kari 1990, undated university pages, or historical programme accounts as current speaker or participant counts.
The publisher of Kathryn Martin’s interview is Native Perspectives on Sustainability. The transcript abbreviation NPS must not be expanded as National Park Service.

Ahtna Heritage Foundation’s work here is evidenced by the 2013 participant study. The apparent ahtnaheritage.org site currently labels itself an unofficial reconstruction and is excluded as a Foundation-authored source.
Keep the archive access discussion explicitly dated to 2013. Do not reproduce archival stories, ritual instructions, taboo rules, or recording contents from these sources.
researchGaps: Current community-approved language teaching offerings, contacts, and access procedures require confirmation from an authoritative community source.
The Mentasta lesson text was inspected, but its audio and interactive functions were not independently listened to or playback-tested.
No first-person interview with present-day language learners was inspected in this batch.
The full 2012 Berez/Finnesand/Linnell archive study, 1975 noun dictionary, and 2010 travel narratives remain unread leads rather than additional counted works.
